claim: A delay's damping byte is one pole inside the delay's own feedback loop, and it is the pole written the cheapest way there is: a running average, one multiply and one state, with no zero at half the rate. Inside rather than once on the way out, which is read off how a held note builds: with the byte at the position the page prints as the filter out the build is 18.3 dB and it is the same in every band, and with the filter in it falls away above a frequency that moves more than four octaves across the byte. A filter outside the loop is the same shape in both windows and cancels between them. That is not the section the same part's chorus filter byte sits on. A pole put through the bilinear transform keeps a zero at half the rate and its skirt bends steeper as it climbs towards it; this one has no zero, so its skirt stops cutting and levels off -- and the profile does level off, on every one of the ten settings the run asked, at a different depth each time. Where a profile levels off names the pole outright with nothing fitted, because the depth is one minus the coefficient over one plus it. Scored through the same takes the cheap pole is sixteen times the bilinear one's median and is the only candidate of eight whose residual does not lean. And it names the clock a fourth time, by a route none of the first three used: the coefficient that puts the corner where the page prints it depends on the rate, so a corner fitted freely from each setting's own skirt lands on the printed third octaves to a five-hundredth of an octave at thirty-two kilohertz and a twentieth at forty-four -- high at every setting, which is a lean and not a scatter. Read on two more types the same byte does one of two things. On the modulated delay it is the same byte doing the same thing: over ten settings and a hundred and thirteen bands the two profiles sit a median 0.045 dB apart, which is under what either run failed to repeat, and the corners agree to a fifteenth of an octave. Nothing was refitted for it -- the claim was closed on one type and reproduced on a second it had never seen. Inside the chorus-and-delay pair it is not. There the profiles sit a median 10.04 dB apart, and the shape is the thing that differs rather than the depth: on both delays the skirt is still falling at the top of the band, by 10.15 dB over the last two octaves at the byte's bottom, while in the pair it has flattened to -0.08 and sits at -24.38 dB from two kilohertz upward. Two explanations for that were tried and both are refused. It is not the run's floor: restricted to the bands where each setting's own take stands twelve decibels clear of its own silence the disagreement is still 10.04 dB. And it is not the held block meaning different things -- the delay time and the feedback on all three types are printed on one conversion column and one hex range, so the same byte is the same quantity, and what differs in the print is each type's own default. What the pair's profile is, is not read here. The claim is a claim about one slot and it now has one type it reaches and one it does not.
named: a one-multiply pole, the running average a fixed-point part damps a delay's repeats with
adds: The record says what this byte did to each twelfth-octave band at ten settings, and carries the steepest slope each was running at. What is read out of it here is that the section is one pole, that the pole is written without the bilinear transform's zero, that this is not the section another type's filter byte sits on, and that the rate the coefficient implies is thirty-two kilohertz. The record names no section, no coefficient and no clock, and says so.
refutedBy: A setting of this byte whose skirt went on cutting past its corner instead of levelling off, which would put the bilinear zero back. Or the depth it levels off at failing to follow the corner the page prints, which is the one thing about this section that is fixed rather than fitted. Or the same sweep on another type's damping byte coming back bilinear, which would make the section this slot's rather than the part's damping routine.

eraPriors.claim: A pole written as a running average costs one multiply and one state; put through the bilinear transform it costs two multiplies and a sample of the input kept beside the sample of the output. What the cheap one gives up is the zero at half the rate, which is a defect in a filter meant to shape a signal and nothing at all in one meant to take the top off a delay's repeats.
eraPriors.why: It says why one part would hold both forms rather than one, which is what the two records together show and what the class's own prior argued against. The prior that a section is written once and reached from more than one byte holds inside a type here and not across the part.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: This byte's skirt had gone on cutting past the corner instead of levelling off, or the chorus's filter byte had levelled off too. Both were measured and each record puts the other's section twelve to sixteen decibels out, so the prior is being carried by a difference rather than by a habit.

alternatives.reading: The same cheap pole clocked at the converter's rate rather than the part's.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: Where its corners land. The coefficient that puts a corner at a given frequency depends on the rate, so a corner fitted freely to each setting's skirt and then held against the third octaves the page prints is a reading of the rate. At thirty-two the ten settings land a median 0.0022 octaves from the series with no sign to them; at forty-four they land a median 0.0548 away and every one of the ten is high, growing from 0.042 octaves at the bottom entry to 0.087 near the top. That is a lean in a quantity the other reading of this same range resolves to about five thousandths of an octave.

alternatives.reading: The section is the bilinear pole the chorus's filter byte sits on, and what levels off at the top of the band is the chain's own floor rather than the section.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The bands where the floor is were taken out before any candidate saw the record, on the record's own admission rule -- a band is scored only where every setting's reading stands ten decibels over the same chain's silence in it, which drops 2 of 113. The bilinear pole is still 11.69 dB out at its worst on what is left, and its freely fitted corners land a median 0.4677 octaves from the printed series -- a third of an octave and more, high at every setting. A floor does not move a corner.

alternatives.reading: Two of the cheap poles cascaded rather than one, which would level off twice as deep.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The skirt, which the reading resolves several times over. Two poles run at twelve decibels an octave where the record's own steepest figures are between two and six, and scored through the same takes the pair is 0.445 against the winner's 0.03 and leans.

alternatives.reading: The damping sits once on the way out of the delay's feedback loop rather than inside it. Queued the other way round, because the record that closed the section could not tell them apart and either was the thing to ask.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The run it queued. A filter on the way out is the same shape in both windows of one take and cancels between them, so it says the build is one number in every band at every setting of the byte -- which is what the position the page prints as the filter out does, at 18.3 dB across the whole band set. Every setting with the filter in departs from that, upward in frequency and by more as the corner comes down: 9.18 dB at setting 32 and 12500 Hz, against 0.41 dB of floor there. And where each setting's build falls through half its depth moves from between 125 and 160 Hz at the lowest setting to between 2500 and 3150 at the highest, which is more than four octaves of something a filter outside the loop cannot move at all.

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// roland-sc8850-01  ·  01 50  ·  filter-section
//
// Generated by yarn sync from inferences/models/0150-one-multiply-pole-at-32k.json.
// The claim it closes: inferences/roland-sc8850-01/0150-a-damping-byte-sits-on-the-cheapest-pole.json
//
// Every constant, every section count and every structural choice below is
// the model's. The difference equations are the ordinary realisations of the
// sections the model names — this site's arithmetic, not a measurement.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

#include <cmath>

namespace soundings::roland_sc8850_01::type_01_50 {

// The same pole written as a running average -- one multiply, one state, no zero at half
// the rate. Its skirt flattens towards Nyquist instead of bending, and where it flattens
// names the pole with nothing fitted.
constexpr double kSampleRateHz = 32000.0;
constexpr double kPi = 3.14159265358979323846;

/**
 * A single pole, written either of the two ways the archive tells apart.
 *
 * `Bilinear` is the transformed pole, which carries a zero at half the rate.
 * `OneMultiply` is the cheapest a fixed-point part can write one — one multiply,
 * one state, and no zero — and the archive holds the two as separate candidates
 * because their skirts differ where it can read them.
 */
struct OnePole {
  enum class Side { Low, High };
  enum class Form { Bilinear, OneMultiply };

  Side side = Side::Low;
  Form form = Form::Bilinear;
  double a = 0.0, c = 0.0, k = 0.0, x1 = 0.0, y1 = 0.0, state = 0.0;

  void set(double hz, Side which, Form how) {
    side = which;
    form = how;
    if (how == Form::OneMultiply) {
      k = 1.0 - std::exp(-2.0 * kPi * hz / kSampleRateHz);
      return;
    }
    const double t = std::tan(kPi * hz / kSampleRateHz);
    c = (1.0 - t) / (1.0 + t);
    a = which == Side::Low ? t / (1.0 + t) : 1.0 / (1.0 + t);
  }

  double process(double x) {
    if (form == Form::OneMultiply) {
      state += k * (x - state);
      return side == Side::Low ? state : x - state;
    }
    const double y = side == Side::Low ? a * (x + x1) + c * y1 : a * (x - x1) + c * y1;
    x1 = x;
    y1 = y;
    return y;
  }
};

// 10 settings read, interpolated in log between them and flat outside them
// read from data/units/roland-sc8850-01/efx-bands/01-50-0A-the-range-that-prints-its-own-null-in-twelfths.json
inline double pole0CornerHz(int byte) {
  static const int kAt[] = {0, 8, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 112};
  static const double kRead[] = {316.067189845, 400.157478413, 500.721471054, 630.413805419, 799.361622273, 1251.88568401, 2004.25528999, 3154.89211578, 5016.90845952, 8025.85878895};
  constexpr int kCount = sizeof(kAt) / sizeof(kAt[0]);
  if (byte <= kAt[0]) return kRead[0];
  if (byte >= kAt[kCount - 1]) return kRead[kCount - 1];
  int i = 1;
  while (kAt[i] < byte) ++i;
  const double t = static_cast<double>(byte - kAt[i - 1]) / (kAt[i] - kAt[i - 1]);
  // The settings were read an octave or so apart, so what sits between two of
  // them is their geometric mean and not their arithmetic one.
  return std::exp(std::log(kRead[i - 1]) + t * (std::log(kRead[i]) - std::log(kRead[i - 1])));
}

// 1 named setting(s) and one value for the rest
inline double pole0Sections(int byte) {
  if (byte == 127) return 0.0;
  return 1.0;
}

/** The chain the model names, in the order it names it. */
struct Effect {
  OnePole pole0[8];
  int poleCount0 = 0;

  void prepare(int b40_03_0A) {
    poleCount0 = static_cast<int>(pole0Sections(b40_03_0A));
    if (poleCount0 > 8) poleCount0 = 8;
    const double poleCorner0 = pole0CornerHz(b40_03_0A);
    for (int i = 0; i < poleCount0; ++i) {
      pole0[i].set(poleCorner0, OnePole::Side::Low, OnePole::Form::OneMultiply);
    }
  }

  double process(double x) {
    for (int i = 0; i < poleCount0; ++i) x = pole0[i].process(x);
    return x;
  }
};

}  // namespace soundings::roland_sc8850_01::type_01_50
